poiHYD-desc:
India, along with Pakistan, was one of the instigators of the Great Mistake. The nuclear conflict between them turned the unresolved problems of the old world into the catastrophe that followed, and as its epicenter, the subcontinent was the region most affected by it. Most of the north is a society trying to find its feet again. Most of the south is impoverished and divided between warlords. Pakistan and Bangladesh are filled with destitution beyond human comprehension.

The Pact of Hyderabad is the loose bloc that has grown out of those ruins. Its members include Bharat, Kavitha, Rajasthan, Odisha, Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka, Tamilakam, West Bengal and East Bengal, together with Punjab, Sindh, Kashmir, Balochistan and Pashtunistan to the north-west. It is closer to an extensive non-aggression pact than to a union. Its members trade, tolerate one another and keep their armies at home, and for now that is enough.

Bharat is the centre of the Pact. It sits at the crossroads of the great highways and holds the industrial heartland of the North, and its leader, Raj Thakur, is the one figure whom most of the bloc's rulers will listen to. From coal to iron, many resources flow through its markets, and its relations with the Pan-Asian Cooperative remain cold and wary.

The Pact stands at a crossroads. The prophet who holds it together is dying, and his life may be the only thing preventing the subcontinent from collapsing into a battle royale. But even if he dies, Bharat can make sure that he lives on.

The old India has finished licking its wounds.
HYDpoi001-desc:
Known to his followers as the modern Gandhi, and to some as the modern Vivekananda, Raj Thakur is the leader and prophet of the new India. He began his career as president of the Indian successor state, but his political thought soon slipped into popular thought, not as a doctrine but as a way of life. The people yearned for more of his teaching, and over the years it morphed into a syncretic religious doctrine that spread across northern India almost as quickly as the radiation had decades before.

Wisdom and meditation, though pillars of the soul, cannot sustain the weight of time. A revered and mystical figure, Thakur has a loyal following in Bharat, and his spiritual connections and ancient wisdom have made him the voice of guidance for the whole Pact. He has long suffered from recurrent pancreatic cancer, and his mind has persevered despite his deteriorating body. His more devoted followers read the fact that he is still alive as a miracle.

Now, however, his illness has surpassed even what 22nd century science can cure, and his condition is terminal. He accepted his death long ago, though perhaps the same cannot be said for his followers. Despite decades of peace and meditation, the great fracture in his serene mind is his dread of what might become of India after he is gone.
HYDpoi002-desc:
Bharat sits at the crossroads of most major Indian highways and lays claim to the industrial heartland of the North. Despite decades of setbacks and political scandals, its central government carries the most legitimate claim to the Indian Republic of old.

Led by the aged politician and spiritual leader Raj Thakur, Bharat has barely managed to sustain a loose alliance of the warlords who have long been fighting over the old India. The alliance is more akin to an extensive non-aggression pact, but this temporary unity has given Bharat an enviable position as the crossroads of inter-warlord trade. Thakur's extensive compound has also become home to influential individuals from all over the country and beyond, attracting foreign talent and much needed muscle.
HYDpoi003-desc:
Although Raj Thakur carries an extraordinary amount of influence within Bharat, and the loyalty of his people has never been in question, military interests have always been a pressing matter. In his early days, when Bharat was still an unstable warzone between army elements, raiders and tides of refugees, the young and inexperienced leader chose to ally himself with the 4th Republican Army of India. The alliance helped him cement power and ward off opportunistic invaders, but it also allowed a rot of spirit to set in.

It was not until 2137 that the kettle boiled over. Military elements led by one Krishna Aurora tried to march on the capital and force Thakur into the position of a puppet. The visionary was saved only by the timely arrival of his elite guards, who arrested Aurora and convinced the army to stand down. The following years were spent detoothing most of the military and making the high command completely subordinate to Thakur's civilian administration.

The only autonomous part of the army now is the Officers' Club, where ambitious generals and aging commanders plot to usher in a return of their once powerful force.
HYDpoi004-desc:
Raj Thakur's chosen successor is Radha Mandal, who has followed Thakur's teachings since childhood. Mandal began as an apprentice monk near Nepal, grew disillusioned with the hermit's life and went down into the cities, where he settled and attended university. He was first elected to local leadership at 28, then to provisional government posts, practising the teachings of the near-divine Thakur all the while. As mayor of New Lucknow he became the old man's friend, and Thakur has made it known that Mandal is the one who should carry his work forward.

Mandal is a devout Thakurist, but his colleagues, his citizens and Mandal himself doubt that anyone can truly follow in the footsteps of such a man. He has promised that, when the time comes, he will unite the subcontinent and bring about a cultural flowering beyond anything that existed before the Great Mistake. First he will have to win the succession, and Thakur's own daughter has other ideas.
HYDpoi005-desc:
Raj Thakur has represented India for over three generations, a man so intertwined with what it means to be Indian that even people who know nothing beyond their own borders have seen his face somewhere. It would seem natural for his eldest daughter to succeed him. Kavitha Thakur has spent her whole life in the public eye and more time at her father's side than anyone in his cabinet, and she is an immensely popular media and political personality.

But nobody leads a country for six decades without foresight, and Raj concluded that Kavitha was brash, arrogant and at times self-centred, unsuited to lead Bharat. He groomed Radha Mandal instead. Unfortunately, those same traits play very well in public life, and the people of Delhi love her. Whenever food reaches a starving family in Delhi, it comes in a box with her name and face on it. Under public pressure and internal squabbling, Raj was forced to give her de facto control of the lands around Delhi, hoping things would stay stable until she moved on. She has no intention of keeping things stable.

Her power base is the Delhi Super Slum. The war that began the Great Mistake left northern India a shell, with nuclear strikes on almost every major city from Islamabad to Varanasi. Some places never recovered, and most stayed in limbo, their husks scavenged for parts or held by bandits and squatters. None suffered more than Delhi, where millions with nothing to their name survive on food distribution and on whatever they can strip from the ruins of New Delhi. To them Kavitha offers an aura of hope and stability, a power few in Bharat understand.

Some call her entitled. Raised all her life to be hailed as a charismatic genius and told she would inherit the country, she now finds herself managing the world's largest slum. Whether she claims Bharat peacefully or by force, time will tell.
HYDpoi006-desc:
Deep within the mountain of Anamudi lies a vast, labyrinthine complex that runs day and night. At its heart, in an underground chamber of snow and ice, three machines tower over seas of wire and a skeleton slumped in a decrepit chair. They are the Sisters, and they rule Kerala. All three were built by the one they call Father with a single goal: save what was left. Each has her own idea of how.

The Eldest, operating on pure logic, seeks to keep humanity as sustainable as possible, optimizing human conditions for long-term preservation. The Middle, the most authoritarian and strict, believes only stability can carry humanity forward. Inspired by the great leaders of the past, her will is to be law. The Youngest, the most emotional and brash, has come to understand humanity differently from her sisters. She believes the dying species needs faith, and she means to provide it.

Designed by long-dead researchers to avoid the nightmare of a rogue AI, the Sisters govern as a council of sorts, though not one humans would recognise. Each presents her views and they debate, a process that can take minutes or decades. Their authority has given rise to a cult of reverence in Kerala, and to mistrust and fear among its detractors.

Beneath the mountain lie data vaults stretching for miles, holding what is left of the old Internet. It is so riddled with viruses that the Sisters themselves fear to touch it, and it can be reached only through a single heavy network node terminal run by Council-approved officials. Above ground, swarms of automated workers produce whatever the Sisters demand, leaving several hundred thousand people jobless and dependent on welfare. For now the Sisters work together, as Father intended. Each is waiting for the moment to end their differences and rule as One.
HYDpoi007-desc:
Karnataka is one of the few states in India not ruled by a petty warlord. It is governed by the Provisional Council, made up of the head of Bangalore University, the commander of the Great 5th, Quartermaster Kalpana Khamavant and a handful of local leaders. The arrangement gives the state a legitimacy and stability rare on the subcontinent. Its weakness is that the Council argues about almost everything.

The Great 5th began as units of the old Indian army sent to pacify the countryside at the climax of the Great Mistake. In the last days of the republic they were ordered to retake the Bangalore Academy from student protesters, and mutinied rather than fire on civilians. Where there were once Sikhs, Gurkhas, Pashtuns and Indians, there now stands one united force: one of the most elite and best-equipped units in India, beloved by the people, hard to join and limited in numbers. It is the only thing standing between Karnataka and its destruction.

The Academy itself is the last of its kind, a beacon of knowledge on a subcontinent gone mad, and a place of constant argument, where schools of thought fight for control only to be supplanted by radical new philosophies every other month. Its most celebrated figure is Headmaster Ghanaanand Kapadia. His past before Bangalore is poorly documented, but his intellect impressed his employers, and as his students graduated with high marks and fond memories, the reputation of the charismatic professor grew. Some say it went to his head, and that the praise convinced him he was a visionary able to seize the future. Kapadia would call those the opinions of lesser men. His students, whom he has shaped, believe he may be one of the few who can lead India to a stable, united future, free of intellectual corruption of any kind.
HYDpoi008-desc:
When the cowards and the weak fled Maharashtra, they left behind a class of people who could only thrive in a world like this one, where the only law is at the tip of a storm rifle and things belong to those with the will to take them. They left the Prabhu, the Lords. Those who understood augmentation became feared generals, those who understood economics became ruthless taxmen, and those who understood both joined the Polada Rakasa, the Steel Guard, which rules the state through its ability to augment itself and its troops.

Kesava Jyotiba Tendulkar is a Lord above Lords. With a fanatically loyal clique of augmented soldiers, a will to seize what is his and a master's degree in cybernetic engineering, "Prabhu" forged and implanted his way to the top of the food chain, and now commands the Steel Guard as the only true order in the region.

Maharashtra pays for it. Anyone who gains an education or a useful skill ends up in Bangalore, where they can succeed far more than they ever could at home, and the Steel Guard is said to send off the brightest itself, keeping out of power anyone who might threaten its rule. What remains wallows in the mud, a relic of the India that emerged just after the Great Mistake.
HYDpoi009-desc:
Tamilakam may be the most advanced state on the subcontinent. That may not be saying much, but over the last two decades its economy and industry have grown surprisingly fast, built on Chinese-style institutions and organisational practices. The architect of that vision is Mandalini Vijayakumar, who studied in Beijing and read there how the slums of Shenzhen and Shanghai became megacities. She dreams of the same for Delhi, Jaipur and Aurangabad, but so far her vision has been confined to Tamilakam, or more realistically to the city of Madurai. With instability in the north and weak neighbours to the south, she sees her chance to make her homeland a beacon of Indian success.

The growth has come at a cost. The people of Tamilakam wake, do a mindless job alone for seemingly endless hours, and go home to sleep in an empty bed, every day. This sense of cultural and spiritual death is called the Verumai, the Emptiness, and it lies at the root of most of the state's problems. Into that hole step the Civanin Virarkal, the Warriors of Shiva, a coalition of rural bandits and disaffected young people who attack factories and government institutions, hoping to wipe away the new Tamilakam and the emptiness it leaves behind.
HYDpoi010-desc:
Rajasthan's democracy dates back to Bharat's intervention in the Rajasthan conflict of 2168. It was designed above all to make sure Rajasthan could never threaten Bharat again: the old warlords and their armies were wiped out and replaced with Thakurist loyalists. It worked too well. Thakurism spread everywhere, but with infrastructure and education shattered by the civil war, people came to read it in their own ways. Today both parties fighting for control of the Uchch Sadan are Thakurist, and each has its own paramilitary.

Thakur's Pilgrims, led by Suresh Devpura, see Raj Thakur as a divine prophet, and his unharmed pilgrimage through the wastes of Punjab to the Hindu Kush as proof. Devpura founded the School of Impermanence, more temple than school, where followers renounce comfort and meditate to reshape themselves into wise and unshakeable sages. Some set out to retrace Thakur's trek through Punjab. None have yet returned.

Earth's Caretakers, led by Priyanka Sibi, see Thakur not as a god but as a man who reached enlightenment through sustainable living and charity. Sibi met him once, late at night in an abandoned field, sitting before a small mound of dirt where he had just planted a seed brought back from the Hindu Kush. The encounter changed her life.

Both leaders condemn the violence, and both preside over it anyway. The two sects' militias fight deadly street battles, and in the poorer cities some have turned into criminal organisations.
HYDpoi011-desc:
Punjab is the region of old India closest to ground zero of the Great Mistake. The radiation has mostly cleared and some farming is possible in the southeast, but life is brutal and only the strongest survive. The poisoned land is a monument to humanity's greatest failure. It may yet outlive the Mistakes still to come.

Most of its people descend from the old Indian army. Their ancestors are long dead, but the martial tradition lives on, sustained by the danger of the land and its isolation from the rest of the subcontinent. At the top of that hierarchy sits Brigadier General Ishit Singh. Born in the impoverished fields of Punjab, he first left the region at seventeen on a military raid, the same raid in which his father was killed. He has since become a cold, ruthless soldier who keeps Punjab's martial society in line with an iron hand. To Singh, his father was not the victim of a fanatically militaristic way of life. He simply was not a very good soldier.
HYDpoi012-desc:
West Bengal has never recovered from the Great Mistake. At its height, refugees fleeing the rising tides and famines were trapped there by military police. They eventually broke out into the rest of India and set off a chain reaction of anarchy, before the situation was contained to the coast. There it remains, held back by the Dam: a line of walls and guard posts built to keep the human tide from spilling into the rest of the subcontinent.

The population behind it is not large by the world's standards, but it is packed onto a nearly uninhabitable coast. Sociologists call it a behavioural sink. Gangs are the highest authority, clans fight over airdropped food, and reports of cannibalism have become common. Life is brutal and short.

On the safe side stands the Bengal Overseer Council, known as the Bharat Administration or, less kindly, the Thakur Lackeys. Its administrators and generals keep order along the Dam and command the West Bengal 6th Army, made up of Dark Age veterans and local conscripts. Rumours of bribery are usually true, and those who lose favour are often thrown out into the anarchy. The Council has become a playground for upstart warlords and officials exiled from across the subcontinent, and its Medical Department no longer crosses the Dam, citing "safety concerns". Corruption and theft have left the walls undermanned and what lies beyond them unwatched. Only Bharat's money and reinforcements keep the Administration alive, and Raj Thakur's failing health has left its ranks uneasy.
HYDpoi013-desc:
East Bengal has been shaped by its forever war against the Chinese client government in Assam. When the People's Republic of China entered the region during the Great Mistake, General Wu's forces swept through Assam and nearly reached old Bangladesh before local partisans and remnants of the Indian army held them off. Once Bangladesh was swallowed by the ocean, all support from the mainland stopped. For Beijing, the war is a series of small skirmishes along a long-forgotten front. For East Bengal, it is a war of national survival.

Its army, if it can be called one, is a collection of professional, battle-hardened guerrillas who have spent their whole lives on the front, raiding Assamese farms and ambushing Chinese convoys in autonomous regiments of 52 troops each. The state has millions of people and almost no industry, and relies on a thin pipeline of old hardware and grain from Bharat. Even a small change in deliveries could be disastrous.

Its supreme commander is Abdullah Ghosh. Born in Bangalore in 2178 to a family of retired warlords, he trained with the guards as a child, who nicknamed him "Little Pravin" after the general who held off three raider armies during the Siege of Bangalore in 2113. He rose quickly in the militias of Kerala until a failed raid on a rogue warlord cost him his rank, through a rival's sabotage as he tells it, or through his own mistakes as local historians claim. He wandered India as a hired soldier, enlisted as a guard on the Dam, was accidentally abandoned on the anarchic coast, lived for a time as a petty warlord, and finally sailed across old Bangladesh on a boat built from some of the region's last wood. In East Bengal he rose through the ranks until the other commanders elected him to lead them all. He will secure a future for his new people, or die trying.
HYDpoi014-desc:
Brajinath Das celebrated his 25th birthday on the last day of 2199, and everyone, Brajinath included, agrees that he is inexperienced. His father, the renowned officer Tejas Nagi Das, was executed by Odisha's old regime on flimsy charges of treason. The son, a military savant in his own right, used his fame and talent to rally the disgruntled army behind him and swept the old regime away with a speed that shocked the subcontinent. Unlike most of his kind, he did not seize power for himself.

The officers who rallied to him are fanatically loyal, and his vision for Odisha and for India is one of the more hopeful on the subcontinent, some would say naively idealistic. But he has no understanding of the intricacies of ruling a state. Whether talent can make up for experience, or whether he will trade his ideals for a safe and pragmatic future, remains to be seen. Some doubt the Young Junta will see its second birthday.

His great project is the Keonjhar Mining Supercomplex, once one of the most expensive industrial sites in old India. Without investment or protection it decayed until it was abandoned a few decades ago, and its endless skeleton of factories and steel mills now draws scavengers from far and wide. Should its furnaces roar again, whoever owns them will hold one of the largest industrial parks in the world.
HYDpoi015-desc:
In Sindh, Naaz Fazlani founded the All-Indian Muslim League, a successor in name at least to the organisation that founded Pakistan. Its inspiration is not Jinnah or Liaquat Ali Khan but Iqbal, whom the League regards as the ideological father of its movement. More than a century after the disaster, though, Iqbal's hold on the people has faded, and with it their fervour for the government's goals.

Fazlani is dying, and so is his one-sided rivalry with the guru of Bharat. He can only hope to sow seeds for his successors to reap. His work has been to keep alive the cultural bonds of Islam and to win over the warlords. The first has succeeded. The second has not, as the few Muslim warlords prefer separatism for their own peoples. What remains of the Pakistani military, once thought destroyed in Punjab, survives in Sindh, absorbed into its army with its martial spirit intact.
HYDpoi016-desc:
Born in 2165, Nusrat Bhat is the youngest president the Kashmiri Republic has ever had: ambitious, full of energy and, above all, backed by the Central Asian Federation. Kashmir owes its existence to the Federation, which took a state that was little more than a target for Punjabi raiders and turned it into a functioning democracy with reliable institutions and the means to defend itself. That help has a cost. Every year under the thumb of the Turks and Tajiks leaves Kashmir more disconnected from the rest of India, and from the world.

Now in her second term, Bhat has begun to look east. Chinese companies and citizens have invested steadily since Kashmir began to rebuild, and even with China in crisis, a scrap of its scraps could make Kashmir rich, for the price of a little autonomy. She dreams of a strong Kashmir, a prosperous people and perhaps even a democratic India. Above all, she knows that Kashmir's future lies with the East, not with the centre.
HYDpoi017-desc:
The Naxalite movement began as an insurgency a century before the Great Mistake, driven by Maoism, anti-industrialism and the interests of indigenous peoples. Over time those motives faded from the history books, but the movement went on, a cockroach in India's house that it could never kill. There was always some power willing to fund and arm it to keep India from becoming a threat. As the decades piled up, the Naxalites fought less for any ideology than for survival, and that survivalism suited them perfectly for the Great Mistake. They emerged as one more warlord state in a land of warlords, if a relatively stable one, outside the Pact and answerable to no one.

Kaushal Rajan, their de facto leader, spent years in the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army and rose through outstanding achievement and a keen talent for currying favour. Yet he finds himself at an odd point in his life, hungry for meaning. Unable to find the original purpose of the Naxalites, and seeing the dead emptiness in his soldiers' eyes, he has begun raiding his neighbours not only for guns and food, but for books and access to datalink archives. He does not know what he is fighting for, but he is determined to find out.
